title: Probing Impurity Quantum Criticality with Entanglement Witnesses
authors: Mateo Cárdenes Wuttig, Andrew J. Millis
abstract: Entanglement is a defining feature of quantum mechanics, and its relation to quantum criticality is of considerable current interest. Here we show that measurable spin and charge fluctuations provide an entanglement witness of quantum criticality in the two-impurity Kondo model, which has experimental realizations in terms of coupled quantum dots and magnetic impurities added to surfaces. We use density-matrix renormalization group and numerical renormalization group calculations to resolve the non-Fermi-liquid critical point separating two independently Kondo-screened impurities from an inter-impurity singlet and interpret it as a change in the dominant entanglement partner of each local moment: from entanglement of the local moment with an extended set of conduction-electron degrees of freedom to entanglement with the other impurity. This reorganization is accompanied by a singular response of the impurity-bath entanglement and the inter-impurity susceptibility. We show how the same structure is encoded in the quantum Fisher information of collective spin and charge operators at zero and finite temperatures, connecting the entanglement picture to experimentally accessible dynamical response functions. Our results establish impurity systems as controlled settings in which quantum-critical entanglement can be detected through measurable correlations, and provide further insight into the possibility of understanding heavy-fermion physics in terms of entanglement.
summary: The paper investigates quantum criticality in the two-impurity Kondo model by using entanglement measures as witnesses. By calculating observables like Quantum Fisher Information and various correlation functions across different coupling regimes, the authors demonstrate that these measurable quantities exhibit singular behavior precisely at the predicted quantum critical point. This establishes a robust theoretical framework for detecting exotic quantum phases in solid-state systems.
main_problem: The study aims to determine if measurable spin and charge fluctuations can serve as entanglement witnesses to detect quantum critical points (QCPs) in impurity systems.
main_result: The analysis confirms that the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), derived from measurable correlations, tracks the entanglement changes across the non-Fermi-liquid QCP separating Kondo-screened and inter-impurity singlet phases.
method: The authors employ advanced numerical techniques like Density-Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) and Numerical Renormalization Group (NRG) to calculate entanglement measures and QFI at zero and finite temperatures.
model_or_system: The primary model is the two-impurity Kondo model, consisting of two spin-1/2 impurities coupled by an exchange interaction ($K$) and each coupled independently to a bath of conduction electrons via Kondo couplings ($J$).
key_observables: Entanglement entropy ($S(A_{	ext{imp}})$), impurity-impurity correlator ($\langle \mathbf{S}_1 \cdot \mathbf{S}_2 angle$), Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) for spin and charge operators.
important_parameters: The critical coupling $K_c(J)$ controls the transition between the Kondo-screened Fermi-liquid state and the inter-impurity singlet phase; temperature ($T$) is also varied.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping entanglement properties onto experimentally accessible dynamical response functions via QFI calculations.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the model setup, showing how various observables like correlators and entanglement measures change across different quantum phases (e.g., 2KS vs IIS).
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the Hamiltonian in different coupling regimes ($J$ vs $K$), calculates ground-state and finite-temperature expectation values using DMRG/NRG, and then maps these results onto entanglement measures and QFI to pinpoint the critical point.
why_interesting: This work directly connects abstract quantum information concepts (entanglement) to concrete, measurable physical quantities (susceptibilities, fluctuations), providing a powerful diagnostic tool for strongly correlated materials like heavy fermions.
